propositions.text: Once Crown establishes conditions, accused must raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability to rebut presumptions.
propositions.quote: once the Crown has established certain conditions, the burden shifts to the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the breathalyzer test results.

propositions.text: If no evidence raises doubt, results presumed accurate and reflect blood alcohol level at material time.
propositions.quote: If there is no evidence raising such a doubt, the results are presumed to be accurate, which is to say that the alcohol level in the breath sample is presumed to reflect the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the time of testing, and that level is presumed to be identical to the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the material time.

paragraphs.summary: Court states accused must raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability to rebut presumptions; otherwise results presumed accurate.

propositions.text: Appeal concerns scope of evidence needed to rebut presumptions of accuracy and identity under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the scope of the evidence that must be adduced to rebut the presumptions of accuracy and identity that are applicable to breathalyzer test results under s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code

propositions.text: Court allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial, with reasons to follow.
propositions.quote: From the bench, the Court allowed the Crown’s appeal from the judgment of the Court of Appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal restored by the Court of Appeal, and ordered a new trial, with reasons to follow.

paragraphs.summary: Court states appeal concerns evidence scope to rebut presumptions; allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial.

propositions.text: Burden on accused to rebut presumptions has been debated but settled by R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux.
propositions.quote: The extent of the burden resting on an accused in such circumstances has been the subject of much debate. In R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57, [2012] 3 S.C.R. 187, this Court put an end to that debate.

propositions.text: To rebut presumptions, accused must show malfunction or improper operation casts doubt on reliability of results.
propositions.quote: Since that decision, it has been settled that to rebut the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C., an accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the approved instrument casts doubt on the reliability of the results (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at para. 52).

propositions.text: New provisions recognize reliability depends on proper operation and maintenance; deficiencies may exist.
propositions.quote: Parliament has recognized that the results will be reliable only if the instruments are operated and maintained properly, and that there might be deficiencies in the maintenance of the instruments or in the test process.

propositions.text: Evidence casting doubt must relate directly to deficiencies to ensure scientific recognition and proper operation.
propositions.quote: What the new provisions require is that evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results relate directly to such deficiencies. This requirement has two purposes. First, it aims to ensure continued scientific recognition of breathalyzer test results, and second, it promotes the proper functioning and proper operation of instruments in order to prevent the reliability of the results from being compromised (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at paras. 33‑36).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains burden on accused to rebut presumptions requires evidence of malfunction or improper operation casting doubt on reliability, per St-Onge Lamoureux.

propositions.text: Accused discharges burden if adduces evidence of improper operation and shows defect tends to cast doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden is discharged if the following conditions are met: (i) the accused adduces evidence relating directly to the malfunctioning or improper operation of the instrument, and (ii) the accused establishes that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Each condition has theoretical and practical elements: procedure generally required and not followed; defect's purpose and effect on reliability.
propositions.quote: Each of these conditions has a theoretical element and a practical element. Therefore, for the improper operation of the instrument to be established, it must first be found that a specific procedure is generally required (theoretical element), and it must then be shown that the procedure was not in fact followed (practical element). The evidence from which it can be inferred that the defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results must be looked at in the same manner.

propositions.text: Theoretical element satisfied if procedure's purpose is to ensure reliability; practical element requires defect could affect reliability in case.
propositions.quote: The theoretical element is satisfied where it is proved that the purpose of the procedure in question is to ensure the reliability of the results. On the practical element, the evidence must establish that, in the particular case, the defect could have affected the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: Court states accused must prove improper operation and defect tending to cast doubt on reliability, each with theoretical and practical elements.

propositions.text: No need to decide if improper operation established; assume it was for argument's sake.
propositions.quote: Even if we assume, without deciding, that improper operation of the instrument was established here based on failure to complete the 15‑ or 20‑minute observation period

propositions.text: No evidence that improper operation tended to cast doubt on reliability of results here.
propositions.quote: there was clearly no evidence that this improper operation tended to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal's judgment reversed; Superior Court's judgment ordering new trial restored.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal’s judgment must be reversed. The Superior Court’s judgment setting aside the verdict of acquittal by the Court of Québec and ordering a new trial must be restored.

paragraphs.summary: Court assumes improper operation but finds no evidence it cast doubt on reliability; reverses Court of Appeal, restores Superior Court order.

propositions.text: On July 12, 2012, respondent stopped, arrested, taken to police station, breathalyzer prepared and control test run.
propositions.quote: On July 12, 2012, the respondent Marc Cyr‑Langlois was stopped by Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau while he was driving his vehicle. Constable Cousineau arrested him at around 12:35 a.m. ... Constable Boissonneault, a qualified technician, went into the breathalyzer room to prepare the instrument and run a control test.

propositions.text: Respondent placed call to counsel confidentially, observed by Constable Cousineau through window.
propositions.quote: Constable Cousineau accompanied the respondent to the interrogation room and then joined Constable Boissonneault in the adjacent breathalyzer room while the respondent exercised his right to counsel confidentially. Constable Cousineau observed the respondent through the window while he placed a call to his counsel

paragraphs.summary: Court recounts facts of respondent's arrest, breathalyzer preparation, and confidential call to counsel observed by officer.

propositions.text: First breathalyzer test at 1:08 a.m. showed 157 mg alcohol/100 ml blood; second at 1:30 a.m. showed 148 mg.
propositions.quote: At 1:08 a.m., Constable Boissonneault gave the respondent a first breathalyzer test, which showed 157 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. ... At 1:30 a.m., Constable Boissonneault administered the second breathalyzer test, which showed 148 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood.

propositions.text: Both results over legal limit; respondent charged with impaired driving and blood alcohol over 80 mg/100 ml; only latter charge at issue.
propositions.quote: Both results were therefore over the legal limit, with a difference of less than 10 mg. The respondent was then charged with operating a motor vehicle while his ability to do so was impaired by alcohol and with operating a motor vehicle with a blood alcohol level exceeding 80 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. Only the second charge is in issue here.

paragraphs.summary: Court states breathalyzer results exceeded legal limit; respondent charged with impaired driving and high blood alcohol; only latter charge contested.

propositions.text: Trial court agreed to first determine if technician breached duty by failing to observe accused for 15 or 20 minutes before tests.
propositions.quote: the court should begin by determining whether Constable Boissonneault had breached the duty to operate the breathalyzer properly by failing to observe the accused himself for a period of 15 or 20 minutes before administering each test.

propositions.text: Accused argued breach rebutted presumptions, requiring acquittal absent Crown evidence.
propositions.quote: The accused argued that, in such a case, the presumptions were rebutted, which had to lead to his acquittal in the absence of additional evidence from the Crown.

paragraphs.summary: Trial court to decide if technician breached observation duty; accused argued breach rebutted presumptions requiring acquittal.

propositions.text: Trial judge found technician not required to observe accused personally; observation by another officer was not continuous.
propositions.quote: the technician was not required to observe the accused himself, the period during which Constable Cousineau had done so was not continuous.

propositions.text: Trial judge found failure to follow observation procedure sufficient to raise reasonable doubt and acquitted accused on second charge.
propositions.quote: his finding that the procedure had not been followed in this case was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt. He did not refer to any additional evidence in this regard. He therefore acquitted the respondent of the second charge

propositions.text: Crown had no evidence to adduce on first charge.
propositions.quote: the Crown stated that it had no evidence to adduce on the first charge.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found observation procedure not followed, raised reasonable doubt, acquitted accused; Crown had no evidence on first charge.

propositions.text: Superior Court allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial.
propositions.quote: the Superior Court, which allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of acquittal and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: Superior Court found trial judge erred in law in acquitting accused, relying on R. v. So principles.
propositions.quote: the trial judge did not properly apply the law and made a fatal error of law in acquitting the [respondent].

paragraphs.summary: Superior Court allowed Crown appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial, finding trial judge erred in law.

propositions.text: In R. v. So, accused must prove deficiency in instrument and that deficiency relates to reliability to rebut presumptions.
propositions.quote: To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused must establish to the reasonable doubt standard: (a) a deficiency in the functioning or operation of the instrument; and (b) that the deficiency directly related to the reliability of the breath test results.

paragraphs.summary: Alberta Court of Appeal in R. v. So summarized accused's burden to rebut presumptions as proving deficiency and its relation to reliability.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal granted leave, heard appeal, majority restored acquittal, dissent would uphold Superior Court.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal set aside the Superior Court’s judgment and restored the verdict of acquittal. ... The dissenting judge would have upheld the Superior Court’s decision

propositions.text: Accused must show improper operation and evidence tending to show it could influence result to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: an accused must not only establish that the breathalyzer was operated improperly, but must also adduce evidence tending to show that its improper operation “[could] influence the result”

propositions.text: Majority found question of fact whether improper operation could influence result; Superior Court erred in intervening.
propositions.quote: this determination essentially concerned a question of fact and that the Superior Court had erred in intervening absent an unreasonable assessment of the evidence by the trial judge.

propositions.text: Dissent found no evidence that deficiency could affect result.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge would have upheld the Superior Court’s decision on the ground that “[t]he [Court of Québec] judge was not faced with evidence showing a deficiency [that could] affect the result”

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal majority restored acquittal finding improper operation could influence result; dissent would uphold Superior Court.

propositions.text: Issue is how accused can show defect tends to cast doubt on reliability when instrument operated improperly.
propositions.quote: The only real issue is how, in cases where there is evidence that an instrument was operated improperly ... the accused can show that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Central dispute is whether purely theoretical evidence suffices to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The heart of the dispute comes down to the following: is evidence that is purely theoretical sufficient for this purpose?

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies issue whether purely theoretical evidence suffices to show defect casts doubt on reliability.

propositions.text: Abstract evidence alone unlikely to meet reasonable doubt requirement; concrete evidence usually required.
propositions.quote: it is more likely that evidence that relates more concretely to the facts in issue will be required. This was the case here: without such evidence, the accused’s argument was in the realm of speculation and could not satisfy the reasonable doubt test

paragraphs.summary: Court finds abstract evidence alone insufficient; concrete evidence usually required to raise reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Respondent argued procedural defect in theory could compromise reliability.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the respondent’s argument that it was enough in this case to show that the procedural defect in issue could, in theory, compromise reliability.

propositions.text: Mere hypothetical possibility insufficient to raise reasonable doubt (R. v. Lifchus).
propositions.quote: Relying on such evidence amounts to accepting a “mere hypothetical possibility”, which is clearly not sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt (R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320, at para. 30).

propositions.text: Respondent was searched twice, monitored, and test results consistent, so digestive issues affecting results unlikely.
propositions.quote: Moreover, it is important to remember that the respondent was searched twice, that he was monitored by the police officers and that the two test results were consistent

propositions.text: Improper operation alleged did not tend to show reliability was in doubt; minimum evidence not adduced.
propositions.quote: The mere improper operation alleged by the respondent did not in itself tend to show that the reliability of the results was in doubt. The minimum evidence required for this purpose was simply not adduced.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects respondent's argument that theoretical defect suffices; finds no evidence reliability was in doubt given monitoring and consistent results.

propositions.text: Improper operation may sometimes alone raise reasonable doubt if serious or closely connected to reliability.
propositions.quote: I do not rule out the possibility that improper operation may be so serious or so closely connected with reliability that it will be sufficient in itself to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results obtained.

propositions.text: Essential that possibility defect affected reliability is serious enough to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: What is essential is that the possibility that the defect affected the reliability of the results is serious enough to raise a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge held concrete evidence must show improper operation may be linked to results, not mere hypothesis.
propositions.quote: concrete evidence must be tendered to show that the improper operation or malfunctioning of the instrument may be linked to the results ... evidence should not be mere hypothesis or conjecture.

propositions.text: Court of Québec judge pointed to no concrete evidence beyond speculation; Superior Court correctly found no evidence casting doubt.
propositions.quote: The Court of Québec judge did not point to any concrete evidence in this regard, and for good reason: beyond conjecture and speculation, the evidence showed nothing. Zigman J. of the Superior Court correctly found that there was no evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal erred in reversing Superior Court's decision.
propositions.quote: the majority of the Court of Appeal erred in reversing his decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court states improper operation may alone raise doubt if serious; finds no concrete evidence here; Superior Court correct; Court of Appeal majority erred.

propositions.text: Intervener argues accused cannot testify about alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1)(d.01).
propositions.quote: An intervener, the Criminal Lawyers’ Association, argues that it would be impossible for an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1) (d.01) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Intervener mistaken; accused can testify about digestive problems as concrete evidence affecting reliability after identifying deficiency.
propositions.quote: The intervener is mistaken. ... an accused who testifies to establish that he or she had a digestive problem is not seeking thereby to show that the instrument was operated improperly. Rather, the accused is providing concrete, rational evidence that the reliability of the results may have been affected, after first identifying a deficiency in the operation of the instrument.

propositions.text: Challenges to presumptions can only be based on proper functioning and operation issues; testimonial evidence admissible but not compulsory.
propositions.quote: It is well established that challenges to the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. can be based only on issues relating to the proper functioning and proper operation of an instrument. ... Of course, the fact that such testimonial evidence is admissible does not make it compulsory.

paragraphs.summary: Intervener argues accused cannot testify about digestive issues; court finds intervener mistaken and allows such evidence after identifying deficiency.

propositions.text: Respondent denies presenting a burping defence, saying it relates only to s. 258(1)(d.1).
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the respondent, who maintains that he did not present a “burping defence” because that defence relates solely to s. 258(1) (d.1) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Burping defence was essential to respondent's argument that improper operation cast doubt on reliability due to unnoticed digestive issues.
propositions.quote: The burping defence was an essential part of his arguments. He argued that the improper operation of the instrument cast doubt on the reliability of the results precisely because ... the police might not notice certain digestive issues that can have a distorting effect

propositions.text: Discussion before trial judge confirms digestive issue was central to respondent's submissions.
propositions.quote: the discussion during the hearing before the Court of Québec judge confirms that this question was central to the respondent’s submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent denies burping defence but court finds it was central to his argument about improper operation and reliability doubt.

propositions.text: No evidence tending to show defect cast doubt on reliability; defect cannot form basis for reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: there was absolutely no evidence tending to show that the alleged defect cast doubt on the reliability of the results. That defect therefore could not form the basis for a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation is a misinterpretation of accused's burden and an error of law.
propositions.quote: acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation reflects a misinterpretation of the accused’s burden of proof, which is an error of law.

propositions.text: Superior Court did not err in setting aside acquittal and ordering new trial.
propositions.quote: The Superior Court did not err in setting aside the respondent’s acquittal and ordering a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence defect cast doubt on reliability; theoretical evidence insufficient; Superior Court rightly ordered new trial.

propositions.text: R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux held evidentiary scheme infringes s. 11(d) Charter right to presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: it was held in R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57, [2012] 3 S.C.R. 187, at para. 27, that the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit infringes the right to be presumed innocent guaranteed by s. 11 (d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms .

propositions.text: Infringement justified partly due to recognized reliability of breathalyzer results, contingent on proper functioning and operation.
propositions.quote: One reason why this infringement is justified in part is because of the recognized reliability of breathalyzer test results. However, the reliability of the results is itself contingent on the proper functioning and proper operation of the instrument.

propositions.text: If accused raises reasonable doubt about proper functioning or operation, presumptions of accuracy and identity must be discarded.
propositions.quote: Where an accused raises a reasonable doubt in this regard, there is no longer any basis for the presumptions of accuracy and identity created by s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code ... and those presumptions must be discarded.

paragraphs.summary: Court recalls St-Onge Lamoureux held evidentiary scheme infringes presumption of innocence but justified by breathalyzer reliability contingent on proper operation.

propositions.text: Trial judge found technician's testimony showed observation period not complied with, raising reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability.
propositions.quote: the trial judge found that the qualified technician’s testimony tended to show that the observation period required prior to the administration of the breathalyzer test had not been complied with and that this was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Acquittal must be upheld as issue is weighing of evidence and no legal error was made by trial judge.
propositions.quote: the trial judge made no error of law that would warrant appellate intervention. The issue is ultimately one of weighing of evidence, and the acquittal must therefore be upheld

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found technician's testimony raised reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability and made no legal error; acquittal must be upheld.

propositions.text: Majority requires evidence showing improper breathalyzer operation caused inaccurate results, e.g., accused's physiological reactions.
propositions.quote: To require, as the majority does in practice, evidence tending to show that the improper operation of the breathalyzer in fact led to inaccurate results — for example, in this case, by imposing an obligation on the accused to testify about his physiological reactions (such as burping)

propositions.text: Such a requirement upsets balance between accused's constitutional rights and Parliament's objectives.
propositions.quote: would upset the delicate balance between the constitutional rights of accused persons and Parliament’s objectives

propositions.text: Recent decision in R. v. Gubbins held breathalyzer maintenance records not available under first party disclosure.
propositions.quote: Coupled with the recent majority judgment in R. v. Gubbins, 2018 SCC 44, [2018] 3 S.C.R. 35, which held that breathalyzer maintenance records are not available under first party disclosure

propositions.text: Requiring evidence of actual inaccuracy would make defences illusory, undermining constitutionality of evidentiary scheme in St-Onge Lamoureux.
propositions.quote: such a requirement would render even more illusory the defences on which the constitutionality of the evidentiary scheme at issue in St‑Onge Lamoureux depends

paragraphs.summary: The court argues the majority's requirement for evidence of actual inaccuracy upsets constitutional balance and undermines defences per St-Onge Lamoureux.

propositions.text: Will discuss St-Onge Lamoureux reasoning, clarify burdens of defence and Crown, consider case facts, and conclude on fairness of new trial.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I will briefly discuss this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux. Then, I will provide some clarification concerning the respective burdens of the defence and the Crown with regard to the functioning and operation of the breathalyzer. I will then consider the facts of this case in order to demonstrate that the original verdict of acquittal is, in my view, unimpeachable. Lastly, I will conclude by emphasizing that it would be unfair to order a new trial given the fact that the Crown is relying on arguments made for the first time on appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court will discuss St-Onge Lamoureux, clarify burdens, analyze facts, and argue a new trial would be unfair due to Crown's new arguments.

propositions.text: Appeal requires considering burden on accused to counter presumptions in s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. and evidence needed to discharge it.
propositions.quote: this appeal requires the Court to consider the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. as well as the type of evidence that the accused must adduce to discharge that burden

paragraphs.summary: The appeal concerns the burden on the accused to counter statutory presumptions and the evidence required.

propositions.text: Position based on majority reasons in St-Onge Lamoureux and recent Gubbins decision.
propositions.quote: My position is based, as it was in the recent decision in Gubbins, on the majority reasons in St‑Onge Lamoureux

propositions.text: Majority acknowledges St-Onge Lamoureux but departs from it in this case.
propositions.quote: the majority also acknowledges the relevance of St‑Onge Lamoureux, but in my view, and with respect, it departs from that decision

propositions.text: Validity of evidentiary scheme upheld partly because accused could raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation.
propositions.quote: the validity of the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit was upheld in part in St‑Onge Lamoureux... because there was still a real possibility that the accused could counter the statutory presumptions by raising a reasonable doubt about the proper operation of the breathalyzer

paragraphs.summary: The court bases its position on St-Onge Lamoureux and Gubbins, noting the majority departs from St-Onge Lamoureux which allowed raising reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation.

propositions.text: Scientific evidence in St-Onge Lamoureux showed breathalyzer reliability but stressed importance of following procedures to ensure accuracy.
propositions.quote: Although the scientific evidence adduced in St‑Onge Lamoureux demonstrated the reliability of breathalyzers, it also highlighted the importance of following the relevant procedures faithfully in order to obtain accurate results

propositions.text: Human error in sample taking and maintenance is real; Hodgson's report emphasizes proper operation and maintenance.
propositions.quote: The possibility of an instrument malfunctioning or being used improperly when breath samples are taken is not merely speculative, but is very real... Hodgson’s report... refers to the importance of proper operation and maintenance

paragraphs.summary: St-Onge Lamoureux scientific evidence showed breathalyzer reliability but stressed importance of proper procedures and acknowledged real human error risk.

propositions.text: Alcohol Test Committee recommends observing accused for 15 minutes before breath sample collection.
propositions.quote: The Alcohol Test Committee... states that before collecting a breath sample, the qualified technician must, among other things, observe the test subject for 15 minutes

propositions.text: Example of relevant procedures ensuring reliability includes observation period before test.
propositions.quote: In discussing the relevant procedures for ensuring the reliability of results, the Court gave the specific example of the period during which the accused must be observed prior to the test

paragraphs.summary: The Court noted the Alcohol Test Committee's recommendation of a 15-minute observation period before breath sample collection to ensure reliability.

propositions.text: Constitutionality depends on whether accused can rebut presumption and how easy it is to do so.
propositions.quote: the constitutionality of the provisions at issue depended, among other things, on “whether it is possible, and how easy it is, for the accused to rebut the presumption”

paragraphs.summary: The constitutionality of the provisions depends on the accused's ability and ease to rebut the presumption.

propositions.text: Only first requirement of s. 258(1)(c) — adducing evidence of malfunction or improper operation — is a reasonable limit on presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: only the first of the three requirements imposed on the accused by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. — that of adducing evidence tending to show that the instrument was malfunctioning or was operated improperly — constituted a reasonable limit on the right to be presumed innocent

propositions.text: This burden justified because results reliable only if instruments operated and maintained properly.
propositions.quote: This burden was justified because it reflected the fact that “the results will be reliable only if the instruments are operated and maintained properly”

paragraphs.summary: Only the burden to show malfunction or improper operation is a justified limit on presumption of innocence, as reliability depends on proper operation.

propositions.text: Court declined to define nature and scope of evidence needed to show improper operation.
propositions.quote: The Court declined to specifically determine the nature and scope of the evidence required to show that the instrument was operated improperly

propositions.text: Deschamps J. noted relevance of Alcohol Test Committee's recommendations indicating instruments may not function optimally if procedures not followed.
propositions.quote: Deschamps J. made a point of noting the relevance of the recommendations made by the Alcohol Test Committee... It can be inferred... that the instruments may not function optimally if the suggested procedures are not followed

paragraphs.summary: The Court did not specify evidence needed to show improper operation but noted Alcohol Test Committee's recommendations imply noncompliance affects function.

propositions.text: Possibility to show procedures not followed means reliability cannot be assumed, justifying first requirement under s. 258(1)(c).
propositions.quote: it was possible for the accused to show that the relevant procedures had not been followed — in which case the reliability of the results could not be assumed — that the Court ultimately concluded that the first requirement imposed by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. was justified

propositions.text: This conclusion clarifies burden on accused to counter statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: that conclusion sheds light on the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions

paragraphs.summary: The Court concluded that the accused can show noncompliance with procedures to rebut reliability, clarifying the accused's burden.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux did not elevate procedural recommendations to statutory conditions for Crown to meet presumptions.
propositions.quote: I am not suggesting that St‑Onge Lamoureux elevated the various recommendations concerning the operation of breathalyzers... to the level of statutory conditions that the Crown must meet to benefit from the presumptions

propositions.text: Only statutory conditions are those imposed by Parliament in s. 258(1)(c)(ii) to (iv).
propositions.quote: The only applicable statutory conditions are those imposed by Parliament in s. 258(1) (c)(ii) to (iv)

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies that only statutory conditions in s. 258(1)(c)(ii)-(iv) apply, not procedural recommendations as conditions.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal majority held accused must only show evidence tending to malfunction or improper operation that could affect reliability, not actual inaccuracy.
propositions.quote: an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions bears only the burden of adducing evidence tending to show a malfunction or improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results; the accused is not required to show that the results are in fact inaccurate

propositions.text: Evidence need only raise reasonable doubt about reliability (St-Onge Lamoureux, Gibson).
propositions.quote: the evidence in question need only raise a reasonable doubt in this regard (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at para. 16; R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 397, at para. 17)

paragraphs.summary: The Quebec Court of Appeal and prior cases hold accused must only raise reasonable doubt about reliability, not prove actual inaccuracy.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires evidence of defect that could cast doubt on reliability, consistent with R. v. So.
propositions.quote: St‑Onge Lamoureux, which simply requires evidence of a “defect that could cast doubt on the reliability of the results”... and with the principles enunciated in R. v. So

paragraphs.summary: St-Onge Lamoureux requires evidence of a defect that could cast doubt on reliability, consistent with R. v. So.

propositions.text: Majority claims burden is to raise reasonable doubt about reliability but requires evidence concretely related to facts, imposing burden to show accuracy doubt.
propositions.quote: majority purports to accept that the burden on the accused is simply to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability... Yet by requiring “evidence that relates more concretely to the facts in issue”... the majority is effectively imposing an obligation on the accused to cast doubt on the accuracy of the results

propositions.text: This is contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux as it resurrects the second requirement of s. 258(1)(c) which was unjustified infringement on presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: I consider it contrary to this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux to impose such a burden, since it amounts to resurrecting... the second requirement in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. It will be recalled that this Court held... this second requirement... constituted a serious infringement of the right to be presumed innocent that could not be justified

paragraphs.summary: The court argues the majority wrongly imposes a burden to show accuracy doubt, contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux's rejection of that requirement.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires reasonable doubt about reliability, not accuracy; these terms differ in meaning.
propositions.quote: St‑Onge Lamoureux requires evidence that raises a reasonable doubt about the reliability rather than the accuracy of the results... these two terms... do not have the same meaning

propositions.text: Reliability means ability to function without incident; accuracy means conformity to truth.
propositions.quote: The former refers, in its technical sense, to the “[a]bility of a system... to function without incident...”; The latter refers to “[c]onformity to the truth”

propositions.text: The distinction between reliability and accuracy is significant in this context.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, this distinction is significant

paragraphs.summary: The court explains St-Onge Lamoureux requires reasonable doubt about reliability, not accuracy, and distinguishes these terms as significant.

propositions.text: Evidence showing malfunction or improper operation increasing possibility of inaccuracy meets accused's burden by affecting reliability.
propositions.quote: where the evidence tends to show... that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the breathalyzer increased the possibility of an inaccurate result, then reliability is affected and the accused has met his or her burden

propositions.text: Accused need only show evidence that a recommended procedure was not followed and that procedure ensures reliability.
propositions.quote: it will be sufficient to adduce evidence tending to show that a recommended procedure was not faithfully followed and that the purpose of the procedure is to ensure the reliability of the results

propositions.text: This is a defect that could cast doubt on reliability per St-Onge Lamoureux; accused's burden ends there.
propositions.quote: this is a “defect that could cast doubt on the reliability of the results” within the meaning of St‑Onge Lamoureux... The accused’s burden ends there

propositions.text: Presumptions justified only if relevant procedures complied with (St-Onge Lamoureux).
propositions.quote: the application of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. is justified only insofar as the relevant procedures are complied with (see St‑Onge Lamoureux)

paragraphs.summary: The accused meets burden by showing procedural noncompliance affecting reliability; presumptions apply only if procedures complied with.

propositions.text: Burden shifts to Crown to prove beyond reasonable doubt that deficiency did not impact accuracy on case facts.
propositions.quote: The burden then shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deficiency in question had no impact on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case

propositions.text: Reverse onus on Crown is not excessive after accused adduces evidence of malfunction or improper operation (St-Onge Lamoureux).
propositions.quote: Deschamps J. noted that there is nothing excessive about this reverse onus: “[B]eing the party that has to prove that there is no connection after the accused has adduced evidence... does not impose a significant additional burden on the prosecution”

propositions.text: If Crown fails burden, it loses benefit of statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: if the Crown fails to discharge this burden, it completely loses the benefit of the statutory presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Crown should not rely on technician rigour to claim reliability then trivialize rigour when reliability challenged.
propositions.quote: [t]he Crown should not be able to rely on the rigour of the technicians to persuade this Court that the results are reliable and then trivialize the importance of that rigour when the reliability of the results is challenged

paragraphs.summary: The burden shifts to Crown to prove no impact on accuracy; failure loses presumptions; Crown should not trivialize technician rigour when challenged.

propositions.text: Accused may rely solely on qualified technician's testimony to raise reasonable doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: There is nothing to prevent the accused from relying solely on the qualified technician’s testimony to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Evidence to counter presumptions may come from Crown or defence witnesses (R. v. Crosthwait).
propositions.quote: evidence to counter the statutory presumptions may be “sought in depositions given by witnesses of the Crown as well as in depositions of defence witnesses”

paragraphs.summary: The accused can rely solely on qualified technician's testimony to raise reasonable doubt, per R. v. Crosthwait.

propositions.text: Qualified technician responsible for proper breathalyzer operation under Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: Under the Criminal Code , the qualified technician is responsible for the proper operation of the breathalyzer

propositions.text: Technician's testimony about not following recommended procedure or uncertainty suffices to raise reasonable doubt without additional evidence.
propositions.quote: where the technician testifies about a recommended procedure... and admits that he or she did not follow the procedure faithfully or does not know whether it was followed faithfully, the accused is not obliged to tender additional evidence

propositions.text: To require corroboration disregards Parliament's unique role for qualified technicians in blood alcohol analysis.
propositions.quote: To take the opposite position would be to disregard the unique role conferred by Parliament on qualified technicians in the context of blood alcohol analysis

paragraphs.summary: Qualified technician's testimony alone can raise reasonable doubt; requiring corroboration ignores Parliament's role for technicians.

propositions.text: The trier of fact must assess evidence to determine if it suffices to counter statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: It is for the trier of fact to assess the evidence adduced in order to determine whether it is sufficient to counter the statutory presumptions.

propositions.text: Qualified technician's testimony alone may not raise reasonable doubt if problems are trivial.
propositions.quote: the trier of fact may well find that, in the circumstances, the qualified technician’s testimony does not in itself raise a reasonable doubt, for example because the problems identified are “frivolous or trivial”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the trier of fact must assess evidence sufficiency to counter presumptions; trivial problems may not raise reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: The trial judge correctly stated the law regarding evidence needed to show breathalyzer malfunction or improper operation.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly stated the law. He properly noted that the accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the breathalyzer was malfunctioning or was operated improperly

propositions.text: Trial judge's factual findings are supported by evidence and verdict of acquittal is unimpeachable.
propositions.quote: His findings of fact on this point are supported by the evidence adduced by the parties. In my opinion, the verdict of acquittal is therefore unimpeachable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge correctly stated law and his factual findings support the acquittal verdict.

propositions.text: The Crown identified no legal error warranting intervention.
propositions.quote: The Crown has not identified any error of law that would warrant this Court’s intervention.

propositions.text: Deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence of procedural non-compliance, not mere speculation.
propositions.quote: it was deprived of the benefit of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. not because of a “mere speculative possibility”, but rather because of concrete and specific evidence showing that a relevant procedure ... had not been followed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legal error; deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence, not speculation, as Crown argued.

propositions.text: Disagrees with majority that trial judge misinterpreted reasonable doubt or based findings on speculation.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with the majority that the trial judge misinterpreted the reasonable doubt standard and that his findings were based on “speculation”

propositions.text: Reasonable doubt must relate to improper breathalyzer operation affecting reliability, not just blood alcohol level or accuracy.
propositions.quote: The reasonable doubt simply had to relate to improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Evidence in this case was not theoretical but concrete regarding breathalyzer operation.
propositions.quote: On this point, the evidence adduced in the instant case was not “theoretical”.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with majority, stating reasonable doubt relates to breathalyzer operation reliability and evidence was concrete, not speculative.

propositions.text: Majority concedes improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt about reliability in some cases.
propositions.quote: the majority concedes that, in certain circumstances, evidence of improper operation may in itself raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Whether evidence suffices to raise reasonable doubt is a trier of fact decision involving sufficiency assessment.
propositions.quote: this is a matter for the trier of fact to decide, since it involves assessing the sufficiency of the evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court notes majority concedes improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt; sufficiency is for trier of fact to decide.

propositions.text: Mr. Cyr-Langlois adduced relevant evidence of improper breathalyzer operation sufficient to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: Mr. Cyr‑Langlois adduced relevant evidence concerning the improper operation of the breathalyzer and the trial judge found that that evidence was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt

propositions.text: This Court should not intervene in the trial judge's decision.
propositions.quote: This Court should therefore not intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent adduced sufficient evidence of improper operation and declines to intervene.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault testified about a 20-minute observation period to ensure no alcohol consumption or physiological reactions before breath test.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault, the qualified technician, himself stated that the procedures prescribed ... include a 20‑minute observation period ... to ensure that the accused has not consumed alcohol, vomited, regurgitated or burped

propositions.text: This testimony sufficed to show a procedure exists to ensure test reliability without needing manuals or expert corroboration.
propositions.quote: This testimony was more than sufficient to show that a procedure exists for ensuring the reliability of the test results. There was no need to file the training manual ... or to have an expert testify

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the technician's testimony about the 20-minute observation period sufficed to show a reliability procedure existed.

propositions.text: Cross-examination showed the accused was not observed continuously during the 20-minute period as required.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault could not confirm that his colleague had observed the accused continuously during the 20‑minute period

propositions.text: There was a period when the accused was alone and unobserved in a soundproof room exercising right to counsel.
propositions.quote: there was a certain amount of time during which Constable Cousineau was unable to determine whether Mr. Cyr‑Langlois burped, since Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was alone in a soundproof room exercising his right to counsel

propositions.text: The qualified technician did not ensure no physiological reactions occurred before testing, despite responsibility.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault does not appear to have been concerned about this, even though he acknowledged that, as the qualified technician, he was responsible for ensuring that no physiological reactions occurred before he took the breath samples

propositions.text: Trial judge could find technician's testimony sufficient to raise reasonable doubt about compliance with observation period.
propositions.quote: the trial judge could certainly find that the qualified technician’s testimony was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about compliance with the prescribed observation period

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence showed the accused was not continuously observed and technician failed to ensure no physiological reactions, raising reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Trial judge could find evidence showed improper breathalyzer operation affecting reliability, not mere possibility.
propositions.quote: it was open to the trial judge to find that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had adduced evidence tending to show improper operation ... and not “simply to show that a deficiency is possible”

propositions.text: This is not conjecture or speculation since technician did not follow prescribed procedure or ensure no physiological reactions.
propositions.quote: this is neither “conjecture” nor “speculation” ... since ... the qualified technician administered the tests without faithfully following the prescribed procedure and without ensuring ... that the accused did not have any physiological reaction

propositions.text: Trial judge could reasonably doubt reliability of results due to improper operation.
propositions.quote: The trial judge could therefore have a reasonable doubt about their reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge reasonably doubted reliability due to improper breathalyzer operation, not mere speculation.

propositions.text: Accused discharged burden under s. 258(1)(c) by raising reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability.
propositions.quote: the accused had discharged his burden under s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal held trial judge was entitled not to extend presumptions without further evidence from accused.
propositions.quote: the first instance judge was entitled not to extend the benefit of the presumptions to the prosecution. He did not have to require anything further from the accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the accused met burden to raise reasonable doubt and cites Quebec Court of Appeal supporting no further evidence required.

propositions.text: Requiring accused to testify about alcohol consumption and physiological reactions after raising doubt would infringe rights.
propositions.quote: it would be contrary to the right to remain silent and the right to be presumed innocent to require an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption and physiological reactions

propositions.text: Majority's approach improperly shifts burden to accused to observe and testify about physiological reactions.
propositions.quote: the majority’s approach shifts the obligation to the accused to observe himself or herself, make note of every physiological reaction and then testify about this

propositions.text: It is the state's responsibility to ensure compliance with conditions for accurate breathalyzer results.
propositions.quote: It is the state’s responsibility, not that of the accused, to ensure compliance with the requisite conditions for obtaining accurate results.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds requiring accused to testify infringes rights and that state must ensure compliance for accurate results.

propositions.text: Majority suggests test result consistency shows observation failure had no impact, confirming reliability.
propositions.quote: The majority suggests that the relative consistency of the two test results ... tends to confirm the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Onus was on Crown to prove observation failure had no impact, which it did not do.
propositions.quote: the onus was on the Crown to prove it ... The Crown did not do so, however, and it must accept the consequences.

propositions.text: Presumptions of accuracy and identity were no longer justified and had to be discarded, leading to acquittal.
propositions.quote: The application of the presumptions ... was no longer justified, and the presumptions therefore had to be discarded. ... the trial judge had no choice but to acquit him.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown failed to prove observation failure harmless; presumptions discarded and acquittal required.

propositions.text: Even if Crown's new arguments were accepted, court would hesitate to order new trial due to their novelty on appeal.
propositions.quote: even if I agreed with the Crown’s position ... I would hesitate to order a new trial in this case

propositions.text: Intervener Association québécoise des avocats et avocates de la défense notes Crown's appellate position differs from trial position.
propositions.quote: the position taken by the prosecution on appeal is clearly different from the one it took at trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Crown's new appellate arguments differ from trial and would hesitate to order new trial.

propositions.text: Crown prosecutor did not argue at trial that technician's testimony alone was insufficient or manuals were needed.
propositions.quote: The Crown prosecutor never argued before the trial judge that the qualified technician’s testimony could not be sufficient in law ... or to introduce evidence of the recommended procedures by filing the relevant training or instruction manuals

propositions.text: Crown did not argue accused had to testify about alcohol consumption or physiological reactions to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: he did not argue that the accused had to testify about his alcohol consumption and physiological reactions

propositions.text: Prosecutor's trial position was that accused was sufficiently observed by officers.
propositions.quote: the prosecutor’s position was that Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau had observed the accused for a period of time that was sufficient in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown's trial position accepted technician's testimony and observation sufficiency, unlike appellate arguments.

propositions.text: Ordering new trial would give Crown a second chance based on new appellate arguments.
propositions.quote: To order a new trial would therefore be to give the Crown a second chance to have Mr. Cyr‑Langlois convicted, on the basis of arguments that were made for the first time on appeal.

propositions.text: Ordering new trial on new arguments may violate double jeopardy principle.
propositions.quote: such a result would be contrary to the double jeopardy principle

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes ordering new trial on new appellate arguments would violate double jeopardy principle.

propositions.text: Trial judge made no reviewable error in finding reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation and countering presumptions.
propositions.quote: the trial judge made no reviewable error in finding that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had raised a reasonable doubt about improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the results

propositions.text: Trial judge did not have to require anything further from accused, per Hogue J.A.
propositions.quote: he “did not have to require anything further from the accused”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in trial judge's decision and agrees accused needed to provide no further evidence.

propositions.text: Majority's approach unduly limits defences based on improper breathalyzer operation.
propositions.quote: the majority’s approach unduly limits the defences based on improper operation of a breathalyzer

propositions.text: Proper defences justify the evidentiary scheme under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: that in fact make it possible to justify the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences ... under s. 1 of the Charter

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority unduly limits proper defences that justify the evidentiary scheme under the Charter.

propositions.text: Majority's reasons rely on Crown arguments made first on appeal.
propositions.quote: the majority’s reasons are essentially based on arguments that the Crown made for the first time on appeal.

propositions.text: Ordering new trial would be inappropriate given circumstances.
propositions.quote: It would be all the more inappropriate, in the circumstances, to order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority relies on new Crown arguments and ordering new trial would be inappropriate.

propositions.text: The court would dismiss the appeal; appeal allowed with dissent by Côté J.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, I would dismiss the appeal. Appeal allowed, Côté J. dissenting.

paragraphs.summary: The court would dismiss the appeal; appeal allowed with dissent by Côté J.
